## Introduction
  
  Netflix publishes its *What We Watched (WWW)* report every six months, beginning from first half of 2023 to the first half of 2026. This report analyzes  *Netflix's What We Watched* data to explore patterns in viewership data, identify the type of content, understand which content captures the most attention and who are the audiences in order to make informed decision making.
  
  The goal is not just to analyze and provide  practical recommendations for Netflix's 2027 content budget but also to help Netflix unlock broader patterns to make more informed decisions about their future investment decisions. 
  
## Data Acquisition
  To begin the analysis, data were loaded from seven *WWW* reports published on *Netflix's  official website* through the code provided by the instructor where these seven reports were  downloaded and saved in a folder `data/mp01` preventing from downloading repeatedly to save processing time. 
  
```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| message: false
#| warning: false
load_netflix_data <- function(){

  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)
  
  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")
    
  if(!dir_exists(data_dir)){
    dir_create(data_dir, showWarnings=FALSE, recurse=TRUE)
  }
  
  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )
  
  download_if_needed <- function(url, local){
    if(!file_exists(local)){
      download.file(url, local, quiet = TRUE, mode = "wb")
    }
    
    return(local)
  }
    
  NETFLIX_URLS |> 
    map(read_html) |> 
    map(html_element, xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]") |> 
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |> 
    enframe("period", "url") |> 
   mutate(path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")), 
          path = map2(url, path, download_if_needed), 
          data = map(path, read_excel, skip=3, na="*"), 
          data = map(data, \(x) x |> mutate(`Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)))) |>
    unnest(data) |> 
    select(-url, -path) |> 
    mutate(year=str_sub(period, 1, 4), 
           half=str_sub(period, start=6), 
           period_start = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 1, 7), 1), 
           period_end = make_date(year, if_else(half==1, 7, 12), if_else(half==1, 30, 31))) |> 
    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |> 
    mutate(live_event = !is.na(Runtime) & str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"), 
           clean_time = str_remove(Runtime, fixed("*")),
           Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) + minute(hm(clean_time))) |>
    select(-clean_time) |>
    mutate(Runtime = coalesce(Runtime, mean(Runtime, na.rm=TRUE)), 
           .by=Title, 
           Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(Title, "Latin-ASCII"),
           Title = str_remove(Title, " // .*"), 
           Title = str_remove(Title, "[^[:ascii:]].*"), 
           Title = str_trim(Title)) |>
    filter(Title != "") |>
    select(year, 
           period, 
           period_start, 
           period_end, 
           Title, 
           -half, 
           Runtime, 
           Views, 
           `Hours Viewed`, 
           `Release Date`,
           `Available Globally?`, 
           live_event) |>
    rename(                 ## Task 2: Fix Column Titles
          title = Title,
          runtime = Runtime,
          views = Views,
          hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
          release_date = `Release Date`,
          available_globally = `Available Globally?`
          )|>                                           # <- pipe added and task 3:Fix column types
    mutate(
      year = as.integer(year),
      available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"
    )
  }
  
  NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()

  
```
 
 Then, the provided code combines the seven reports into a single data frame called `NETFLIX_DATA` that has **`r scales::comma(nrow(NETFLIX_DATA))`**  rows and **`r ncol(NETFLIX_DATA)`** columns which will be used for rest of this mini project. 
  
## Data Cleaning and preparation

 Before starting analysis,the raw data needed some clean-up or fixes. The column names look quite messy and some date types are incorrect. To get valid `R`column names, column names were converted to lowercase with underscores (e.g. `Hours Viewed` = `hours_viewed`). Similarly, data type for `year`was converted to integer, and `available_globally` was converted from `"Yes"`/`"No"` string values to `TRUE`/`FALSE` logical values. All of these changes were made  directly into `load_netflix_data()` function above. 
 
```{r}
#| label: verify-cleaning

glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```
 
## Exploratory Analysis

### Initial Data Exploration  
 Before answering any questions, as a part of exploratory analysis, I wanted to get the sense of data and ran two basic checks on the cleaned data: one for column types and one for summary statistics.

#### Check 1: Column types

```{r}
#| label: Data_Exploration_glimpse

glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```
Absolutely, the data types are now as expected. The `year` column is now an integer, `available_globally` and `live_event` are logical, and  `period_start` and `period_end` are dates.

#### Check 2: Summary Statistics

```{r}
#| label: Data_Exploration_skim
 library(skimr)
 skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
 
 miss <- sapply(NETFLIX_DATA, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
 print(miss)
print(exists("miss"))
med_hours <- median(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
max_hours <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
``` 

From the summary statistics we can see that cleaned Netflix dataset is comprised of four variable data types: **character variables** (`period` and `title`), **date variables** (`period_start`, `period_end`, and `release_date`), **logical variables** (`available_globally` and `live_event`) and **numeric variables** (`year`, `runtime`, `views`, and `hours_viewed`). 

The major finding here is missing data: `release_date` has **`r scales::comma(miss[["release_date"]])`** values missing, `views` has **`r scales::comma(miss[["views"]])`**, and `runtime` has **`r scales::comma(miss[["runtime"]])`** values missing which might limit analysis to some extent. Thus, `hours_viewed` has no missing values which can be used as a most reliable key measure for measuring titles popularity.

Moreover, it is important to know that `hours_viewed` is rounded and is highly right skewed with median of **`r scales::number(med_hours / 1000000, accuracy = 0.1)` million hours**, meaning half of the titles has viewing hours below this value and half has above this value, although very few popular titles have significantly high viewing hours of **`r scales::number(max_hours / 1000000, accuracy = 0.1)` million hours**, much higher than the median. Hence, using median in the analysis prevents the popular titles from affecting the results too much. 


### Task 5- Exploratory questions

The given six exploratory questions provide quick overview of Netflix's viewing data across titles. The R code below calculates Netflix's summary statistics to examine the dataset's time frame, the number of titles, the popularity of two popular franchises, the share of total viewing hours of the top 10 most watched titles, and the worldwide reach of the Netflix's titles. 

```{r}
#| label: task5-values

# Q1: date range (period_end is off for H1 periods, so derive the end date)
first_date <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)
last_date  <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start) + months(6) - days(1)

# Q2: number of distinct shows and movies (seasons count separately)
n_titles <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$title)

# Q3: total hours for the Bridgerton universe

bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Bridgerton")) |>
  summarise(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q4: total hours for the five Stranger Things seasons
stranger_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(str_detect(title, "Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Beyond Stranger Things")) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, regex("Tales from", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  filter_out(str_detect(title, "Fireplace")) |>
  summarise(total = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(total)

# Q5: share of 2026H1 watch time spent on that period's ten biggest titles
h1_2026 <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(period == "2026H1")
top10_share <- h1_2026 |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  summarise(top10 = sum(hours_viewed)) |>
  pull(top10) / sum(h1_2026$hours_viewed)

# Q6: share of the catalog that is globally available
# By title: every title-period listing counts once
global_by_title <- mean(NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally, na.rm = TRUE)

# Weighted by hours viewed
global_by_hours <- weighted.mean(
  NETFLIX_DATA$available_globally,
  NETFLIX_DATA$hours_viewed,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

The analysis shows that the *WWW* dataset covers the period from **`r format(first_date, "%B %d, %Y")`**, to **`r format(last_date, "%B %d, %Y")`** and contains **`r scales::comma(n_titles)`** different shows and movies across given seven periods, with each season counted individually.

Similarly, the *Bridgerton* franchise recorded **`r scales::comma(bridgerton_hours)`** hours of viewing, including all titles containing "Briderton". Whereas, the five main seasons of  *Stranger Things* recorded **`r scales::comma(stranger_hours)`** hours, excluding the companion titles *Beyond Stranger Things: Beyond 2*, *Stranger Things: Tales From '85: Season 1*, and *Stranger Things: Fireplace*.

In terms of viewing concentration, the top 10 titles accounted for **`r scales::percent(top10_share, accuracy = 0.1)`** of total viewing hours in the first half of 2026. globally available titles recorded **`r scales::percent(global_by_title, accuracy = 0.1)`** of all title listings but represented **`r scales::percent(global_by_hours, accuracy = 0.1)`** of viewing hours. This indicated that globally available titles attract a larger share of viewing hours than of the total titles in the dataset.

Overall, this summary provide a general picture of Netflix's catalog, viewing trends, and the global content availability. 

### Task 6: Exploratory Questions - Table Answers

```{r}
#| label: load-gt
#| message: false

library(gt)
```
#### 1. What was the top show (by total hours viewed) in each period and what fraction of total viewership did it capture?

```{r}
#| label: task6-Question1

top_repeat <- top_by_period |> count(title, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1)
top_repeat_periods <- top_by_period |>
  filter(title == top_repeat$title[[1]]) |>
  pull(period)
top_max <- top_by_period |> slice_max(share, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
n_top_titles <- n_distinct(top_by_period$title)
top_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(period_total = sum(hours_viewed), .by = period) |>
  slice_max(hours_viewed, n = 1, by = period, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(share = hours_viewed / period_total) |>
  select(period, title, hours_viewed, share) |>
  arrange(period)

top_by_period |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", title = "Top Title",
             hours_viewed = "Hours Viewed", share = "Share of Period Viewing") |>
  fmt_number(hours_viewed, decimals = 1, suffixing = TRUE) |>
  fmt_percent(share, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "The Most-Watched Title and Its Share of Viewing Hours by Period") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

The table shows that the most-watched title varied across different reporting period with `r top_repeat$title[[1]]` leading across two reporting period `r paste(top_repeat_periods, collapse = " and ")`. `r top_max$title[[1]]` recorded the highest share accounting `r scales::percent(top_max$share[[1]], accuracy = 0.1)` in `r top_max$period[[1]]`. Since no top-watched title exceeded 1.4% of viewing hours, it suggest that viewership was distributed across different reporting period rather than being concentrated throughout the periods. Note: Low-viewership titles are omitted in the analysis.


#### 2. How has Netflix’s catalog changed in size over the periods for which we have questions? You should consider both the number of titles and the total runtime of content.

```{r}
#| label: task6-Question2

catalog_size <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(n_titles = n(),
            total_runtime_hours = sum(runtime, na.rm = TRUE) / 60,
            .by = period) |>
  arrange(period)

catalog_size |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period", n_titles = "Titles Reported",
             total_runtime_hours = "Total Runtime (hours)") |>
  fmt_number(c(n_titles, total_runtime_hours), decimals = 0) |>
  tab_header(title = "[Catalog size and Runtime Over Time]") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

#### State: This counts titles that appear in the reports, not Netflix's full library, because titles under the viewing threshold are left out. Runtime is missing for some titles and is excluded from the sum.

#### 3. Which shows have had the most consistently high viewership across all periods? These shows are likely to be ‘staples’ that viewers fall back on as ‘comfort food’, e.g., re-runs of Friends.

```{r}
#| label: task6-Question3

n_periods <- n_distinct(NETFLIX_DATA$period)

staples <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(periods_present = n_distinct(period),
            avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
            min_hours = min(hours_viewed),
            sd_hours = sd(hours_viewed),
            .by = title) |>
  filter(periods_present == n_periods) |>
  mutate(cv = sd_hours / avg_hours) |>
  slice_max(min_hours, n = 10)

staples |>
  select(title, avg_hours, min_hours, cv) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(title = "Title", avg_hours = "Average Hours",
             min_hours = "Lowest Period", cv = "Variation (SD / Mean)") |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, min_hours), decimals = 1, suffixing = TRUE) |>
  fmt_number(cv, decimals = 2) |>
  tab_header(title = "[Comfort-food staples]") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

##### State: Your rule in plain words. Mine is "present in all periods, ranked by the weakest period," because a title with a high minimum never dipped. The variation column shows consistency. Requiring all periods is strict, because a title just under the reporting threshold would drop out.

#### 4. Within each period, what fraction of time was spent on ‘shows’ vs movies?

```{r}
#| label: task6-Question4

typed <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(content_type = case_when(
    live_event ~ "Live event",
    str_detect(title, "Season") ~ "TV show",
    runtime > 240 ~ "TV show",
    .default = "Movie"
  ))

type_share <- typed |>
  summarise(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .by = c(period, content_type)) |>
  mutate(share = hours / sum(hours), .by = period) |>
  select(period, content_type, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = content_type, values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(period)

type_share |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(period = "Period") |>
  fmt_percent(-period, decimals = 1) |>
  tab_header(title = "[Shows versus movies]") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

##### State:
The heuristic: "Season" in the title, or runtime over 240 minutes, means TV show. Live events get their own category so they don't distort the movie share.
"Fraction of time" means share of hours viewed, not runtime.
Rows with missing runtime and no "Season" land in "Movie". Check how many that is with typed |> filter(is.na(runtime)) |> count(content_type).
Shows like "Stranger Things 4" have no "Season" in the title and are caught only by the runtime rule.

#### 5. How does the performance of live events compare to pre-taped content? Does the average live event draw more viewership than an average piece of pre-taped content? How about a ‘top tier’ live event vs ‘top tier’ pre-taped content?

```{r}
#| label: task6-Question5

live_compare <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(type = if_else(live_event, "Live event", "Pre-taped")) |>
  summarise(n_titles = n(),
            avg_hours = mean(hours_viewed),
            median_hours = median(hours_viewed),
            top10pct_hours = quantile(hours_viewed, 0.9),
            best_title_hours = max(hours_viewed),
            .by = type)

live_compare |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(type = "Type", n_titles = "Titles", avg_hours = "Average Hours",
             median_hours = "Median Hours", top10pct_hours = "90th Percentile",
             best_title_hours = "Best Title") |>
  fmt_number(n_titles, decimals = 0) |>
  fmt_number(c(avg_hours, median_hours, top10pct_hours, best_title_hours),
             decimals = 1, suffixing = TRUE) |>
  tab_header(title = "[Live events versus pre-taped content]") |>
  tab_source_note("Source: Netflix What We Watched reports")
```

##### State:
How you defined "top tier": I used the 90th percentile and the single best title. Say which you chose.
How many live events there are. If it's only a handful, the averages are noisy.
Live events are single sittings, while shows add up many hours of runtime, so raw hours favor long content.

## Memo calculations
These are supporting calculations for the memo preparation.

###  Burstiness calculation

```{r}
#| label: memo-burstiness

# period_end is off for H1 in the scaffold, so rebuild it
burstiness_data <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(period_end_fixed = period_start + months(6) - days(1)) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(release_date),
    release_date >= period_start,
    release_date <= period_end_fixed
  ) |>
  mutate(
    days_available = as.integer(period_end_fixed - release_date) + 1,
    availability_group = case_when(
      days_available <= 14 ~ "0-14 days",
      days_available <= 30 ~ "15-30 days",
      days_available <= 90 ~ "31-90 days",
      .default = "91+ days"
    ),
    availability_group = factor(
      availability_group,
      levels = c("0-14 days", "15-30 days", "31-90 days", "91+ days")
    ),
    hours_per_day = hours_viewed / days_available
  )

burst_summary <- burstiness_data |>
  summarise(
    n_titles = n(),
    median_total_hours = median(hours_viewed),
    median_hours_per_day = median(hours_per_day),
    .by = availability_group
  ) |>
  arrange(availability_group)

burst_new  <- burst_summary |> filter(availability_group == "0-14 days")
burst_mid1 <- burst_summary |> filter(availability_group == "15-30 days")
burst_mid2 <- burst_summary |> filter(availability_group == "31-90 days")
burst_old  <- burst_summary |> filter(availability_group == "91+ days")

burstiness_ratio <- burst_new$median_hours_per_day[[1]] /
  burst_old$median_hours_per_day[[1]]

total_share_new_vs_old <- burst_new$median_total_hours[[1]] /
  burst_old$median_total_hours[[1]]

n_burst_rows   <- nrow(burstiness_data)
pct_burst_rows <- n_burst_rows / nrow(NETFLIX_DATA)
```


### Live Event values

```{r}
#| label: memo-live

# Live-flagged titles and their share of viewing, per period
live_by_period <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    n_live = sum(live_event),
    live_share = sum(hours_viewed[live_event]) / sum(hours_viewed),
    .by = period
  ) |>
  arrange(period)

first_live <- live_by_period |> filter(n_live > 0) |> slice(1)
last_live  <- live_by_period |> slice_tail(n = 1)

# One row per live-flagged title, across all periods
live_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(live_event) |>
  summarise(hours = sum(hours_viewed), .by = title) |>
  arrange(desc(hours))

top_live_title <- live_titles$title[[1]]
top_live_hours <- live_titles$hours[[1]]
next14_hours   <- sum(live_titles$hours[2:15])

# WWE grouping is a keyword rule on title names
wwe_pattern       <- "Raw|WrestleMania|Royal Rumble|WWE|SmackDown"
wwe_titles        <- live_titles |> filter(str_detect(title, wwe_pattern))
wwe_share_of_live <- sum(wwe_titles$hours) / sum(live_titles$hours)
wwe_title_share   <- nrow(wwe_titles) / nrow(live_titles)
n_wwe_in_next14   <- sum(str_detect(live_titles$title[2:15], wwe_pattern))

# First period: how much of it is one fight?
live_2024h2        <- NETFLIX_DATA |> filter(live_event, period == "2024H2")
tyson_share_2024h2 <- max(live_2024h2$hours_viewed) / sum(live_2024h2$hours_viewed)

# defining live_share_min and live_share_max
live_share_min <- min(live_by_period$live_share[live_by_period$n_live > 0])
live_share_max <- max(live_by_period$live_share[live_by_period$n_live > 0])
```

## Corporate Strategy Memo: Netflix Content Strategy for 2027 and beyond

To: Netflix leadership

From: Strategy Analyst

Date: October 2026

Subject: Improving New Releases and Live Programs

### Recommendation

Netflix may rely on viewing data to make better decisions about its content. This report prioritizes two critical sections: how quickly new releases attract viewers and how many audiences watch live programs? Netflix should prioritize on promoting new titles when they are first released and carefully evaluate its live programs. 

### 1. Prioritize new releases

The data show that titles available for 0-14 days has a median of `r scales::comma(burst_new$median_hours_per_day[[1]], accuracy = 1000)` viewing hours per day while the titles released for 91 days and more received a median of `r scales::comma(burst_old$median_hours_per_day[[1]], accuracy = 1000)` hours per day, meaning new titles received about `r round(burstiness_ratio, 1)` times more viewing hours per day. In simple terms, the newest title tends to get more attention shortly after release but it does not necessarily support that the title's popularity degrade over time. 

However, titles available longer tend to have higher total viewing hours which suggest that although new titles attract viewers more quickly, older titles continue to accumulate viewing hours over a longer period.

**Strategic Actions**: Netflix should invest heavily on promotional activities for selected titles during first two weeks of releases and see the performance before applying the same strategy for rest of the releases. However, it is important to consider the fact that release date information has missing values which may not accurately represent the true picture.

### 2. Carefully Evaluate Live Programming

Netflix should continue exploring different live events separately before drawing conclusion on where to invest in 2027. The data show that live-flagged titles have increased from `r first_live$n_live[[1]]` in `r first_live$period[[1]]` to `r last_live$n_live[[1]]` in `r last_live$period[[1]]`. However, their share of total viewing hours remained within `r scales::percent(live_share_min, accuracy = 0.01)` to `r scales::percent(live_share_max, accuracy = 0.01)`. This means overall share of viewing hours remained quite small although the number of flagged titles increased.

The data also showed that Jake Paul vs. Mike Tyson show had `r scales::comma(top_live_hours, accuracy = 100000)` viewing hours more than the rest of the combined top-titles in the list `r scales::comma(next14_hours, accuracy = 100000)`)” (next 14 live-flagged titles combined). WWE programs also accounted for `r scales::percent(wwe_title_share, accuracy = 1)` of live flagged titles and `r scales::percent(wwe_share_of_live, accuracy = 1)` of live flagged viewing hours suggests that WWE is important part of Netflix's content and worth evaluating for the upcoming investment plan

**Strategic Actions:** Netflix should not mix one-time live event with recurring  programs because comparing these measures can help Netflix identify the most viewing and identify consistent audience interest before making investment decisions. Netflix should consider that viewing hours data has limitations as it cannot alone measure profitability as the dataset does not include revenue, costs or subscriber details. 

## Conclusion

For 2027 and beyond, Netflix should find ways to attract more viewers when new titles are released and strategically plan its promotional activities for content investments. Alongside, it should use performance data to evaluate live programs while also considering cost and revenue data (which is currently unavailable) before Netflix actually decides whether further investment is worthwhile.
